'''Cohl Furey''', also known as '''Nichol Furey''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Deffke |first=Uta |orig-date=05 January 2021 |title=The octave magician: Nichol (Cohl) Furey is a researcher at IRIS Adlershof |url=https://www.adlershof.de/en/news/the-octave-magician/ |website=adlershof.de |publisher=Adlershof Journal |location=Berlin}}</ref> is a [[Canadians|Canadian]] [[mathematical physics|mathematical physicist]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |last=Wolchover |first=Natalie |author-link=Natalie Wolchover |date=July 20, 2018 |title=The Peculiar Math That Could Underlie the Laws of Nature |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-octonion-math-that-could-underpin-physics-20180720/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220321075337/https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-octonion-math-that-could-underpin-physics-20180720/ |archive-date=21 March 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/quantas-year-in-physics-2018-20181221/ |title=The Year in Physics |first=Natalie |last=Wolchover |author-link=Natalie Wolchover |date=December 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424042730/https://www.quantamagazine.org/quantas-year-in-physics-2018-20181221/ |archive-date=24 April 2022 }}</ref>

==Career==
Furey has a bachelor's degree in mathematics and physics from [[Simon Fraser University]] (2005), Master's degree from the [[University of Cambridge]] (2006) and a Ph.D in theoretical physics from the [[University of Waterloo]] (2015).<ref>{{Cite web |title=N. Furey - CV |url=https://www.furey.space/_files/ugd/96fef8_ffeb7b7cba26499f91d19c237a037b81.pdf |access-date=2023-08-13}}</ref> She was a research fellow at the University of Cambridge's [[Trinity Hall, Cambridge|Trinity Hall]] from 2016 to 2019<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 24, 2022 |title=Women in STEM: Dr Cohl Furey; University of Cambridge |url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/women-in-stem-dr-cohl-furey |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424042833/https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/women-in-stem-dr-cohl-furey |archive-date=24 April 2022 |website=}}</ref> and spent a few months at the [[African Institute for Mathematical Sciences]] in [[Cape Town]]. Since 2020, she has been at the [[Humboldt University of Berlin]] on a Freigeist Fellowship by the [[Volkswagen Foundation]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Project description: In-depth study into the algebraic structure of elementary particle physics |url=https://portal.volkswagenstiftung.de/search/projectDetails.do?ref=96182 |access-date=2023-08-13 |website=VolkswagenStiftung}}</ref>

Her main interests are [[division algebra]]s, [[Clifford algebra]]s, and [[Jordan algebra]]s, and their relation to [[particle physics]]. Her work focuses on finding an underlying mathematical structure to the [[Standard Model]] of [[particle physics]]. She is most noted for her work on [[octonion]]s.<ref name="ideals" /><ref>{{cite journal | title=Generations: three prints, in colour | first=C. J. | last=Furey | journal=[[Journal of High Energy Physics]] | date=2014-10-07 | doi=10.1007/JHEP10(2014)046 | volume=2014 | issue=10 | page=46 | arxiv=1405.4601 | bibcode=2014JHEP...10..046F | s2cid=13813401 }}</ref><ref name="generations" />

She has worked on attempting to obtain the Standard Model of particle physics from octonionic constructions.<ref name="auto" /><ref name="ideals">{{cite journal|last=Furey |first=Cohl |author-link=Cohl Furey |title=Unified theory of ideals |date=2012-07-20 |journal=[[Physical Review D]] |volume=86 |issue=2 |article-number=025024 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.86.025024 |arxiv=1002.1497 |bibcode=2012PhRvD..86b5024F|s2cid=118458623 }}</ref><ref name="generations">{{cite journal|last=Furey |first=Cohl |author-link=Cohl Furey |title=Three generations, two unbroken gauge symmetries, and one eight-dimensional algebra |journal=[[Physics Letters B]] |volume=785 |date=2018-10-10 |pages=84–89 |doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2018.08.032 |bibcode=2018PhLB..785...84F|arxiv=1910.08395 |s2cid=126205768 }}</ref> In her 2018 paper "''SU''(3){{sub|''C''}} × ''SU''(2){{sub|''L''}} × ''U''(1){{sub|''Y''}} (× ''U''(1){{sub|''X''}}) as a symmetry of division algebraic ladder operators,"<ref>{{cite journal|last=Furey |first=Cohl |title=''SU''(3){{sub|''C''}} × ''SU''(2){{sub|''L''}} × ''U''(1){{sub|''Y''}} (× ''U''(1){{sub|''X''}}) as a symmetry of division algebraic ladder operators |journal=European Physical Journal C |volume=78 |date=2018-05-12 |issue=5 |page=375 |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-018-5844-7  |doi-access=free|pmid=30996664 |pmc=6435233 |arxiv=1806.00612 }}</ref> according to ''[[Quanta Magazine]]'', "she consolidated several findings to construct the full Standard Model symmetry group, [[Mathematical formulation of the Standard Model|SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1)]], for a single generation of particles, with the math producing the correct array of electric charges and other attributes for an [[electron]], [[neutrino]], three [[up quark]]s, three [[down quark]]s and their [[antiparticle|anti-particles]]. The math also suggests a reason why [[electric charge]] is quantized in discrete units — essentially, because whole numbers are."<ref name="auto" /> In 2022 together with Mia Hughes, she linked the [[symmetry breaking]] in physics to division algebras including octonions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brooks |first=Michael |date=August 2022 |title=Octonions: The strange maths that could unite the laws of nature (=Reality's hidden depths) |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/0-octonions-the-strange-maths-that-could-unite-the-laws-of-nature/ |journal=New Scientist |language=en |volume=255 |issue=3400 |pages=38–41 |doi=10.1016/S0262-4079(22)01494-4}}</ref>

==Media recognition==
In 2019, ''[[Wired.com]]'' listed her in their article "10 Women in Science and Tech Who Should Be Household Names".<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.wired.com/story/10-women-science-tech-household-names/ |title=10 Women in Science and Tech Who Should Be Household Names; WIRED |first=Emily |last=Dreyfuss |author-link=Emily Dreyfuss |date=March 8, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308180339/https://www.wired.com/story/10-women-science-tech-household-names/ |archive-date=8 March 2022 }}</ref>
